chapter: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
title: Hinton's tribute and Wilson's honorary doctorate
summary: Hinton says record companies neglected Wilson and praises his dignity; Wilson mentions his Berklee honorary doctorate.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: You know, you and I have been doing this during this road trip and it's fabulous, and performing a number of years now. And I've mentioned about the dignity that you've always carried. You were the epitome of the jazz musician, you've given dignity to this music, which it's been so sorely needed.

And I've mentioned so many times that -- and this is a little moment of me saying, I thought you've been neglected by these big recording companies here when your records did so much to make these companies get the -- big companies here like Columbia. And yet they don't find -- with all their they don't find time to give you a contract to record. But you go to Japan, to Europe in order to do things. You're one of the few jazz persons that's kept the dignity of the jazz. And I know you see jazz -- it's been very nice for us here recently, where we can go and perform and do concerts.
You just recently got a doctorate, where'd you get your doctorate from? Wilson
Oh, that's from the Berklee College of
music, an honorary Doctor of Music degree from Berkeley Lee College in Boston.

I was thinking it was about time. But I'm so thrilled to know this because you have lent so much class to it, like we mentioned before, being the first black in an interracial band and being able to perform and carry that dignity, maintain that -- great people like you --
